explanations.explanation: Shearing is right, friend. Nabal, a wealthy man from Maon, is shearing his sheep in Carmel. The text says he has a thousand goats and three thousand sheep. That's a lot of haircuts, and I can barely keep my own mustache in line.

Nobody mentions a market here, friend. The text says Nabal, a wealthy man from Maon, is shearing his sheep in Carmel. He has a thousand goats and three thousand sheep, so he's got plenty of wool to deal with.

I get why counting comes to mind with that many animals. But the text says Nabal, a wealthy man from Maon, is shearing his sheep in Carmel. It does give the numbers, a thousand goats and three thousand sheep, but the work in front of him is shearing.
The text says the opposite, friend. Abigail is described as intelligent and beautiful. Her husband Nabal, a Calebite, is called harsh and evil in his dealings.
False is right, baker. Abigail is described as an intelligent and beautiful woman. Her husband, a Calebite, is called harsh and evil in his dealings. Kind and generous isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: A wish for long life and peace
explanations.explanation: That's how it opens, friend. David tells the young men to say, “Long life to you, and peace to you and to your house and to all that belongs to you.” That's a warm hello before any request. I'd take that greeting over a lot of emails I've seen.

David does ask for something, but not first. The greeting opens with a blessing: “Long life to you, and peace to you and to your house and to all that belongs to you.” The request for whatever Nabal can spare comes later in the message.

No raider warning in this message, friend. David's young men are told to greet Nabal in his name and say, “Long life to you, and peace to you and to your house and to all that belongs to you.” It's a friendly opener from start to finish.
True, baker. David's message says, “Ask your young men, and they will tell you.” He's inviting Nabal to check the story with his own people. He points Nabal to his own workers for the answer.
It's actually true. David's message says, “Ask your young men, and they will tell you.” He points Nabal to his own workers to confirm it. The invitation is right there in the message.
That's it, friend. The message says, “Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.” It's a modest ask on a feast day. David doesn't name a number or a price.
That would be a big ask, friend, and David doesn't make it. The message says, “Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.” He leaves the amount up to Nabal.
Land never comes up. The message says, “Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.” It's about what Nabal can spare on a feast day, nothing more.

explanations.answer: He asks who David even is
explanations.explanation: Yep. Nabal says, “Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse?” He answers a friendly greeting with a question that sounds like he's never heard the name. Friend, that's a rough way to answer someone wishing you peace.

explanations.answer: He invites David to the feast
explanations.explanation: There's no invitation, baker. Nabal asks, “Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse?” The men came with a blessing and went back with a brush-off.

explanations.answer: He promises David a small gift
explanations.explanation: No gift is promised. Nabal asks, “Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse?” Then he asks why he should give away his bread and water and meat at all.

Shearers is it. Nabal says, “Why should I take my bread and water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give them to these men whose origin I do not know?” He says he doesn't know these men's origin, and that's the question he asks about giving them anything.
Close to home, but no. Nabal says he slaughtered the meat “…for my shearers…” Those are the men who work his flocks. The word he uses is shearers, not family.
Soldiers would sound more dramatic, friend, but that's not the word. Nabal says he slaughtered the meat “…for my shearers…” These are the men working his flocks.
That's the order. David says, “Strap on your swords!” And all his men strap them on. Friend, the mood in that camp just changed fast.

explanations.answer: Let it go and move on
explanations.explanation: David does the opposite. He says, “Strap on your swords!” He doesn't let it go. About four hundred men follow him.
No second message goes out. David says, “Strap on your swords!” and about four hundred men follow him. A hurt greeting turns into a march.

True, baker. Nabal's young man tells Abigail, “They were a wall around us, both day and night, the whole time we were herding our sheep near them.” A wall is a pretty strong picture of being watched over. It's his own worker saying so.

It's true, friend. Nabal's young man tells Abigail, “They were a wall around us, both day and night, the whole time we were herding our sheep near them.” Those words come right from Nabal's own household.

Disaster is the word. The young man says, “…disaster looms over our master and all his household.” He's telling Abigail to think carefully about what she must do. Friend, when a servant says that, you listen.
Not famine, baker. The young man says, “…disaster looms over our master and all his household.” The warning is about the trouble Nabal's words have stirred up.
Sickness isn't the word, friend. The young man says, “…disaster looms over our master and all his household.” He wants Abigail to think carefully about what she must do.
The text says otherwise, friend. Abigail tells her young men to go ahead of her, but verse 19 says she “…did not tell her husband Nabal.” She acts quietly and quickly.
False is right, baker. The text says she “…did not tell her husband Nabal.” She sends her young men ahead and follows right behind them.

explanations.answer: Leave no male of his alive
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it's a heavy one. David says, “May God punish David, and ever so severely, if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning.” That's a serious oath. I think this is the moment the story holds its breath.

It goes way past sheep, friend, and it's a heavy moment. David swears, “May God punish David, and ever so severely, if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning.” He's talking about people, not property.

Driving someone out isn't what he swears, and it's a heavy moment. David says, “May God punish David, and ever so severely, if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning.” That's far more serious than an eviction.
She doesn't hide at all, friend. When Abigail sees David, she quickly gets off her donkey, falls facedown and bows before him. She walks straight toward the problem.
False is right, baker. Abigail sees David and quickly gets off the donkey, falls facedown and bows before him. No hiding in the ravine for her.
True, friend. At David's feet, she says, “My lord, may the blame be on me alone, but please let your servant speak to you…” She asks to carry the blame herself. Then she asks to be heard.
It's true, baker. Abigail falls at David's feet and says, “My lord, may the blame be on me alone…” She asks to carry it herself before she says anything else.
Fool is right, friend. Abigail says of Nabal, “His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.” That's his own wife speaking, right to David. She says it to ask David to pay him no attention.

Proud is a fair guess for a man who snaps at messengers, but it's not the meaning Abigail gives. She says, “His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.” She says it to David as she asks him to pay Nabal no attention.
He is rich, friend. The text tells us about the thousand goats and three thousand sheep. But Abigail says, “His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.”

Bloodshed is the word. Abigail says the LORD “…has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand…” She credits the LORD with stopping David. Friend, that's one brave thing to say to a man with four hundred swords.
Not weariness, baker. Abigail says the LORD “…has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand…” She's talking about David's oath, not his energy.

Hunger isn't it, friend, even though Abigail did show up with a big load of supplies. She says the LORD “…has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand…” The word is bloodshed, not hunger.
That's what she says. Abigail tells David, “…the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles.” She's looking far down the road for him.

David already has men following him, but that's not the promise. Abigail says, “…the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles.” The promise is a dynasty, baker, not an army.
No palace is mentioned, friend. Abigail says, “…the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles.” A dynasty is a lot bigger than a building.
True, baker. Abigail says that when the LORD has done all the good He promised, “…He has appointed you ruler over Israel…” She says it to David face to face. That's a big thing to hear in a ravine.
It's true, friend. Abigail speaks of the day “…when He has appointed you ruler over Israel…” She says it out loud to David.
That's her last request. She says, “And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant.” After all that, it's a small, humble ask.
She never asks him to leave. Her last words are, “And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant.” Her request is to be remembered, not to see him go anywhere.

explanations.answer: That he pay for the gift
explanations.explanation: No payment, friend. She's giving the gift freely, and her last request is, “And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant.” What she asks for is to be remembered.

explanations.answer: The LORD the God of Israel
explanations.explanation: Right. David says, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day!” He gives the credit to the LORD for the meeting. That's a big turn from a man who was strapping on a sword.

Samuel is a good guess, but he had already died at the start of this chapter. David blesses “…the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day!” The blessing goes to the LORD, not to a prophet.
Saul, Israel's king, isn't part of this meeting at all, friend. David says, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day!” The blessing goes to the LORD.
Yes. David says, “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request.” He receives what she brought and sends her off in peace. That's his answer after hearing her out.
He doesn't invite her along. He says, “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request.” He sends her home, baker, not off to Carmel with his men.
He doesn't ask her to stay. David says, “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request.” Then she heads back home.

True, baker. Abigail finds Nabal in high spirits and very drunk, so she tells him nothing until morning light. She tells him in the morning, when he's sober. That's the day after a feast fit for a king.
It's true, friend. When Abigail gets home, Nabal is in high spirits and very drunk. The text says, “So she told him nothing until morning light.”
That's it. When Nabal hears, “…his heart failed within him, and he became like a stone.” It's a heavy moment, so I'll say it plainly. I think this one hurts.
No rage this time. The text says, “…his heart failed within him, and he became like a stone.” It's a heavy moment, friend.
No tears or apology are mentioned. The text says, “…his heart failed within him, and he became like a stone.” It's a heavy moment.
That's what the text says. About ten days later, “…the LORD struck Nabal dead.” This is a serious moment, friend, so I'll leave it plain.
David's attack never happens. The text says that about ten days later, “…the LORD struck Nabal dead.” That's a serious line, friend.
Moving away isn't what the text says. It says that about ten days later, “…the LORD struck Nabal dead.” It's a heavy line, baker.
Yes. David says, “For the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” It's about Nabal's own wickedness. David also says the LORD “…has restrained His servant from evil.”
No famine here, friend. David says, “…the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” The thing brought down on Nabal is his own wickedness.
David's sword isn't what the text names, friend. He says, “…the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” He also thanks the LORD for restraining him from evil.
Wife it is. David sends word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife. His servants then come to her at Carmel and say, “David has sent us to take you as his wife.”
She did give good advice, friend. But David's message asks her to become his wife. So the word is wife, not advisor.
Ally is a fair guess after that meeting in the ravine. But David asks her to become his wife. So the word is wife, not ally.
The text shows the opposite, friend. Abigail “…hurried and got on a donkey…” She follows David's messengers with five of her maidens. No taking her time here.
False is right, baker. Abigail hurried, got on a donkey and followed David's messengers. No dawdling, just a woman on the move.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. So she and Abigail were both his wives.” Abigail isn't the only one, and the next verse calls Michal David's wife too.
False is right, baker. The text says David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. So Ahinoam and Abigail were both his wives.
True, friend. Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim. That's the closing verse of the chapter. It still calls Michal David's wife.
It's true, baker. Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim. That's how the chapter closes. The text still calls Michal David's wife there.
